readingInstruction: Read Psalm 105:1-22 slowly, twice. This is one of the Psalter’s great historical psalms. It walks through the story of God’s faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants. Read it as the appropriate response to the Abrahamic covenant story you have been encountering.
settingTheScene: Psalm 105 is one of the longest historical psalms in the Bible. It rehearses God’s saving acts from Abraham to the conquest of Canaan. Today’s reading covers the first 22 verses, from the covenant with Abraham through the early years of Joseph in Egypt. The psalm is essentially a hymn-form summary of Genesis 12-41 and a preparation for the Exodus to come. It teaches the people of God how to remember and how to give thanks.
observation: The psalm opens with calls to give thanks, sing, and tell, worship as proclamation.
Verse 8 is the theological hinge: “He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations.”
Verses 9-10 specifically name the covenants with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the patriarchal line.
Verse 11 quotes God’s promise: “To you I will give the land of Canaan as your portion for an inheritance.”
The patriarchs are called “few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it.” Their smallness is part of the wonder.
Verses 14-15: “He allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, ‘Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm.’” God protected them.
Then the psalm pivots to Joseph: “He sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave.” God’s sovereignty in suffering.
interpretation:
Psalm 105:1-22 is a worship-form summary of everything you have been reading in Genesis. It begins with the call to remember, to give thanks, to sing, to tell. And then it remembers, by rehearsing the story of God’s covenant faithfulness to Abraham and his offspring.

Verse 8 is the central claim. “He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations.” This is the antidote to the despair that often accompanies covenant life. The patriarchs lived through famine, infertility, betrayal, slavery. They lived in a land that was not yet theirs. They saw children but not grandchildren of the promise. And yet, through all of it, God remembered. The Hebrew word for remember in Scripture is not passive recollection. It is active loyalty. When God “remembers” his covenant, he is acting in faithfulness to it. The psalm announces that this remembering is not just for one generation. It is for a thousand. Forever.

Verses 9-11 quote the Abrahamic promise directly. The covenant with Abraham was confirmed to Isaac and renewed with Jacob. It is a single, unfolding promise, the same God to the same family with the same word about the same land. And verse 11 puts in God’s own mouth: “To you I will give the land of Canaan as your portion for an inheritance.” This is what Abram believed in Genesis 15, and what God reckoned to him as righteousness.

Then the psalm becomes startlingly honest about the smallness of the patriarchs. “When they were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people.” This is the truth about Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. They were not powerful. They were not numerous. They were nomads, vulnerable to every famine and every local king. And yet, the psalm says, “he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account.” Pharaoh in Egypt, Abimelech in Gerar, God protected the patriarchs even from the most powerful men of their day. He still does this with his people. We are few. We are weak. We are sojourners. And he protects us.

The psalm then turns to Joseph. “He sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave.” This is the heart of the Joseph story before Joseph even reaches Pharaoh’s house. God sent Joseph. Joseph was sold by his brothers, betrayed, enslaved, imprisoned, but God sent him. The same God who promised Abram a great nation arranged for Joseph to be in Egypt so that the family could later be preserved through famine. What looked from the ground like tragedy and injustice was, from heaven’s perspective, sovereign provision. This is the doctrine of providence in narrative form. And we will see it played out in full when we read Joseph’s story in the next two weeks of this plan.
connection: The first chapters of Unit 3 have introduced the patriarchs, Abraham primarily, with Isaac and Jacob and Joseph yet to come in greater detail. Today’s psalm teaches us how to receive these stories. They are not just family history. They are the record of God’s covenant faithfulness, remembered for a thousand generations. As the unit unfolds, we will see the patriarchs at their best and at their worst. Psalm 105 reminds us that the story is ultimately about the God who remembered, not about the people who were remembered.
application:
Make remembering a habit. The Christian life is not primarily about discovering new truths but about remembering old ones, that you were lost, that you were redeemed, that you are loved, that you are kept. Today, recall one specific way God has been faithful to you in the past. Name it. Thank him for it. Tell someone about it. This is what the psalmist commands: give thanks, sing, tell the deeds of the LORD. Worship is, in large part, memory exercised.

And take comfort from the smallness of the patriarchs. They were few. You may feel few. They were of little account in the world’s eyes. You may feel of little account. They were sojourners. So are you. And the same God who protected them protects you. He has not forgotten his covenant. He remembers, for a thousand generations.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for remembering his covenant, and for remembering you in Christ.
Tell him about a season that feels like famine or slavery, and ask him to preserve you through it.
Ask him to teach you to tell of his works.
